issue.title: gateway: request-body write can stall forever on a reused HTTP/2 connection — no timeout applies and the group never fails over
issue.body:
## Summary

On 2026-10-21, requests from this host (magpie `v0.1.1290`, macOS, loopback `127.0.0.1:3425`) to an HTTP/2 upstream (`opencode.ai`, provider `opencode`) stalled **while writing the request body**. Nothing in magpie bounded the wait:

- `ResponseHeaderTimeout: 10 * time.Minute` never fired, because the request was never fully written (`TryNet.Send` ≈ the whole duration; `TryNet.Wait`/`Head` absent).
- The routing group's next member was never asked — the group has no `firstToken` set (`0` = "waits as long as it takes"), while the other member (`deepseek/deepseek-flash`, direct) was healthy and answering in ~1–2 s the whole time.
- The only bound was the client's own cancel: Hermes kills a stream after 900 s with no chunks; one user turn stayed stuck from 14:11:56 to 15:18:56 (five consecutive stale attempts, then abort).

This looks like the write-phase sibling of #2529 (per-provider first-byte stall timeout) and #2843 (group requests hang indefinitely).

## Environment

- magpie `v0.1.1290`, built from pinned upstream `1a3b9268` with three unrelated local safety patches (managed-key fail-closed, searcher off, auto provider migration disabled); macOS, gateway `127.0.0.1:3425`
- HTTP/2 upstream: `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/chat/completions`
- Group `auto-deepseek-flash`: `["opencode/deepseek-flash", "deepseek/deepseek-flash", "opencode/deepseek-v4-flash"]`, no `firstToken`
- Client: streaming chat completions with a ~500k-token prompt (request body of a few MB)

## Observed (from `data/routing/<date>.jsonl`, `tries[].net`)

| try start | status | ms | net.send | net.wait | net.head | net.reused |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 14:11:57 | 499 (client cancel) | 899937 | 899533.9 | – | – | true |
| 14:26:58 | 499 | 410611 | 410116.4 | – | – | true |
| 14:33:49 | 499 | 900209 | 899674.8 | – | – | true |
| 14:48:50 | 499 | 900056 | 899645.4 | – | – | true |
| 15:03:52 | 499 | 900156 | 899637.8 | – | – | true |

Healthy control, same body, same day: `send=3650 ms`, `wait=13064.7 ms`, `head=17431.8 ms`, status 200.

One request with a smaller body finished its write and then hit the header timeout exactly as designed: `502 ... http2: timeout awaiting response headers` after `600280 ms`.

## Why the current guards don't cover it

- `internal/gateway/upstream_transport.go`: `ResponseHeaderTimeout` starts only after the request is written; `replayable` retries only when the kept-alive connection is *found dropped* (EOF / broken pipe). A socket that stays open and makes no progress raises no error and no retry.
- `internal/gateway/nettrace.go`: `Send` = "writing the request, headers and body"; `Wait` = "from the request written to its reply's first byte" — the routing log shows the stall is in `Send`.
- `internal/provider/group.go`: `FirstToken` is opt-in (`0` waits forever); `Patience` only replans after failures that pass (busy / overloaded / rate limited), not a silent hang. The last member left is always waited for.

## Ask

1. Bound the write phase: e.g. a write/upload deadline on the upstream transport (or fold "time to the reply's first byte, request included" into one deadline) so a black-holed connection cannot hold a request until the client cancels.
2. Make the stall trigger existing failover: with `Group.FirstToken` set, a member that has produced no first content within N seconds should be let go and the next member asked (already implemented — consider defaulting it for groups, or at least surfacing it when unset).
3. Consider closing the connection after a write stall instead of keeping it for reuse.

## Notes

- Related: #2529 (per-provider first-byte stall timeout), #2843 (group hang), #1421 (bounded retries / nested group failover).
- Full local evidence (routing extracts, `usage.jsonl`, client-side logs) available; happy to provide or test a build.

comments.body:
The write phase had no bound. `net/http`'s `ResponseHeaderTimeout` starts only once a request is written, so a vendor that leaves the connection open and stops reading the body — its HTTP/2 stream's flow-control window never opens again — held the request until your client cancelled, and because nothing failed, the group never asked its next member. The connection keeps answering pings, so `netproxy.HTTP2Health` (#2843) has nothing to drop either.

The branch bounds the write the way the first-byte wait is bounded: `writeBounded` in `internal/gateway/upstream_transport.go` lets a request go when the transport has taken nothing more of its body for a minute (`upstreamWriteStall`), by cancelling that request's own context. The try fails with `the vendor stopped taking the request for 1m0s`, so the group asks its next member; the stalled HTTP/2 stream is reset and the connection kept. Each read the transport takes puts the bound back off, so a slow upload that keeps moving is never cut, and `WroteRequest` ends it, leaving the wait after a written request to `ResponseHeaderTimeout` as before. Requests with no body are untouched. It sits on the vendor transport, so it covers every request magpie sends a vendor (relayed, translated, embeddings, a drawing), not only a chat turn.

[fix/3191-gateway-request-body-write-can](https://github.com/skygunner/magpie/tree/fix/3191-gateway-request-body-write-can), commit 043fe4effa17d02a3cff01861d217aea9058488e

Run: `TestStalledRequestWriteLetsTheGroupMoveOn` — your case as a fixture, a 4 MB prompt body to a local HTTP/2 server that reads none of it; red before the change (`200 ` after 10.007s, hung until the client's own timeout), green after (`ok internal/gateway 0.189s`), and 5 runs under `-race` with no flake. Also `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/gateway/`, and the two #2843 tests beside it under `-race`. The whole `internal/gateway` suite was started and did not finish, so it has no result either way.

This is a fork branch, ready to review; it makes no claim on the issue's ownership.

Additional field report from another environment, with a similar symptom on a newer Magpie build.

## Environment

- macOS arm64
- Magpie `0.1.4334` when the incident started; it auto-updated to `0.1.4335` on 2026-11-17
- Local gateway: `127.0.0.1:3425`
- Model: `gpt-6.1-sol`
- Three custom OpenAI Responses-compatible providers, all pointing to the same internal relay (provider names and endpoint redacted)
- Routing group: `auto-gpt-6-1-sol`, `routing=fast`, concurrent Pi/Codex/Hindsight streaming requests
- Prompt sizes range from roughly 50k to 500k tokens

## Observed with HTTP/2 enabled

- Intermittent HTTP/2 `GOAWAY`, `closed network connection`, and stalled response-body reads
- Goroutine snapshots contained `golang.org/x/net/http2`, `http2.transportResponseBody.Read`, and Magpie's `netproxy.h2Watch.Read` stacks
- Requests were eventually cancelled by the client after tens of seconds to several minutes; Magpie logged HTTP 499 with `the agent canceled the request`
- The local Magpie process was not CPU- or memory-bound

## Workaround and remaining behavior

Setting `http1=true` for all three custom providers removed the new HTTP/2 goroutine blocks and I have not seen new GOAWAY/closed-connection signatures after the switch. Requests are much more stable, but long requests can still end as client-cancelled 499s while uploading or waiting for the upstream.

A single isolated curl probe was slightly faster over HTTP/2 than HTTP/1.1 (about 3.15s vs 3.91s total), so forcing HTTP/1.1 is a reliability workaround rather than a raw performance improvement. The failure appears specific to Magpie's reused HTTP/2 connections and concurrent long-lived SSE traffic.

## Context-size evidence

The time spent sending the request body grows sharply with prompt size in this environment:

- `<50k` tokens: about 40ms median
- `50k-150k`: about 1.37s
- `150k-300k`: about 4.3s
- `300k-450k`: about 8.1s
- `>=450k`: about 23.7s median; total latency around 39.5s median

This makes a global `groupFirstToken=8-10` risky: a large prompt may still be uploading when the first-token timer fires, causing the same multi-hundred-thousand-token body to be uploaded again to the next provider.

## Questions

1. Does the request-body write-stall fix discussed in this issue cover custom providers that share one HTTP/2 upstream endpoint and connection pool?
2. Is there a planned per-provider HTTP/1.1 fallback or write-stall/first-byte timeout that resets a stuck reused HTTP/2 stream and then lets the group fail over?
3. Could the gateway distinguish upload/write stalls from model-side first-token latency, so large requests do not need an aggressive global first-token timeout?

I can provide redacted routing extracts, timing data, and stack snapshots if useful. No API keys, request bodies, or internal hostnames are included here.

issue.title: 上下文超限之后，不要把同一份请求原样丢给下一个成员

repository.name: magpie
repository.description: Every agent's model. One place. Codex on DeepSeek, Claude Code on Kimi, from the menu bar.

issue.body:
Pi 走路由组 `auto/deepseek-v4.1-flash`（WorkBuddy 的 DeepSeek，然后是 Ollama Cloud）。会话大了之后，一次请求先在 WorkBuddy 上耗了 161 秒，得到：

```text
prompt is too long: 100001 tokens > 100000 maximum
```

接着同一份请求又被传给 Ollama，上传 108 秒后返回 `failed to read request body`（ref: ae788d94）。模型没开始生成。12:25 还有一次一样的（ref: 795c3344），Ollama 那次传了 217 秒。

WorkBuddy 目录里写的窗口是 100 万，实际第一次没缓存时只收 10 万。缓存接上之后，同一条会话到 24 万也能过。Ollama 也不是坏了：旁边一条已经有缓存的会话，25 万 token 只新增 222，返回 200。

这和几条已有 issue 是一件事：

- #3337：同样的 100001 > 100000。那边只有一个成员，会话被钉死，重发不再换人。
- #1404：上游说超了，本地只数出大约 8 千，于是每次都先问一个必然拒绝的成员。
- #1944：超限被当成限流，同一份超大请求又试一遍。
- #3191、#711：连接卡住、413 这种是成员没接住，同一份请求换下一家是对的。

超限和没接住不是一种失败。429、5xx、鉴权失败、写 body 超时、413，请求本身没被判超，换下一家。上游明确说 `N > M`，或者 `context_length_exceeded`，就把 M 记成这个成员的真实上限，只交给已知上限更大的成员。没有这样的成员，就把错误还给客户端去压缩，不要再传一遍。

选路时用这个上限，不用目录里的 100 万。本地计数只拿来跳过明显装不下的，以上游返回的 M 为准。会话亲和也只在这个成员装得下、缓存还在时保留。超限一次就解开，避免 #3337 那种重发永远打回同一个后端。

issue.title: gateway: all requests to an HTTP/2 upstream share one connection and queue on its flow-control window (TTFT 1 s → 150–270 s under load)

repository.name: magpie
repository.description: Every agent's model. One place. Codex on DeepSeek, Claude Code on Kimi, from the menu bar.

issue.body:
## Summary

All requests to an HTTP/2 upstream share one connection, so under concurrent load with large request bodies they queue on that connection's HTTP/2 send window. Time to first token went from ~1 s to 150–270 s, even though the upstream, the key and the network path were all fast when tested on their own. As far as we can tell there is no setting to use HTTP/1.1 or more than one connection for a provider.

Related, but not the same problem: #2843 (the shared connection went dead; fixed by the health ping) and #3191 (a body write stalls completely). In our case the connection is alive and the uploads keep moving, just very slowly, so neither the health ping nor a write-stall timeout fires.

## Environment

- magpie v0.1.3332 (`ghcr.io/yetone/magpie@sha256:a70569f3…`), `magpie serve` in a Linux x86_64 container (GKE, asia-northeast1)
- One custom provider: Alibaba Bailian's Anthropic-compatible endpoint (`https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/apps/anthropic`, served over HTTP/2), model `deepseek-v4.1-flash`
- Clients: several DeepSeek Harness (`dsh --profile headless`) agents through the gateway with per-client gateway keys. Each turn sends a request body of about 1.1 MB. Up to about 9 requests are in flight at once.

## Measurements (2026-11-09, same key, same tiny prompt, streaming)

| Path | Time to first byte / total |
|---|---|
| Laptop → Bailian directly | 0.6 s / 0.8 s |
| Inside the magpie pod, `curl` → Bailian directly (bypassing magpie) | 1.7–1.9 s / 3.0 s |
| Inside the magpie pod, `curl` → `127.0.0.1:3425` (magpie) → Bailian, during load | 25–48 s total (`ttft_ms` 25 786 / 37 400 in `usage --csv`) |
| Same request through magpie that morning, with little load | 0.76 s total |
| Real agent turns through magpie during load (`usage --csv`) | `ttft_ms` 138 000–270 000, `duration_ms` 150 000–515 000, status 200 |

magpie's CPU use was about 20m at the time, so it was not busy. It was waiting.

## Where the requests wait (`magpie goroutines`)

Every upstream request is on the same `*http2.ClientConn` (`0x2e07282b96c0`). Some streams wait for headers and others for send window:

```
goroutine 13185 [select, 3 minutes]:
golang.org/x/net/http2.(*ClientConn).internalRoundTrip(0x2e07282b96c0, ...)
	golang.org/x/net@v0.56.0/http2/transport.go:1030
...
github.com/yetone/magpie/internal/netproxy.calmAlt.RoundTrip(...)          calm.go:105
github.com/yetone/magpie/internal/gateway.rpmTransport.RoundTrip(...)      rpm.go:291
github.com/yetone/magpie/internal/gateway.(*Server).forwardOnce(...)       gateway.go:5918

goroutine 13197 [sync.Cond.Wait]:
golang.org/x/net/http2.(*clientStream).awaitFlowControl(0x2e0729cac000, 0x4000)
	golang.org/x/net@v0.56.0/http2/transport.go:1661
```

The dump had 8 goroutines in `internalRoundTrip` on that one `ClientConn` (waiting 2–4 minutes) and 3 in `awaitFlowControl`. We can attach the full dump if it would help.

## Why we think this happens

`x/net/http2` only opens another connection when the server's `MaxConcurrentStreams` is reached. Being starved of flow-control window does not make it open a new one. With large bodies and a server that keeps a small connection window, total upload speed is capped at about window ÷ RTT for **all** clients together. Every concurrent request makes the others wait longer, and long-running streamed replies keep the queue full. The same request on its own connection, without magpie, takes about 3 s from the same pod.

## What we would like

Any one of these would solve it for us:

1. A per-provider option to use HTTP/1.1 upstream, so each request gets its own pooled connection.
2. A per-provider connection pool for HTTP/2, either with a set number of connections or one that opens a new connection when streams are waiting on flow control.
3. A larger initial connection/stream window, if the slowdown turns out to be on the receive side for long streamed replies.

For now we have moved our heavy agents off the gateway and call the upstream directly.

- Magpie `0.1.4334` when the incident started; it auto-updated to `0.1.4335` on 2026-11-17
- Local gateway: `127.0.0.1:3425`
